# Change and adjacency {#lagoa-change}

## Transitions between dates {-}

Knowing how much each class grew or shrank does not tell you where the area
went. `land_change()` answers that question by comparing the maps pixel by
pixel, at two or three dates, and measuring what stayed, what was converted and
into what:

```{r change, fig.height=6.5}
change <- land_change(maps, years = c(1985, 2024), language = "en")
change$plot
```

```{r include=FALSE}
im <- change$interval_metrics
cm <- change$class_metrics
f3 <- cm[cm$code == 3, ]
```

```{r echo=FALSE}
top <- cm[order(-cm$gross_change_ha), ][1:5, ]
tabela(data.frame(Class = top$class, `1985 (ha)` = top$initial_ha, `2024 (ha)` = top$final_ha,
                  `Gain (ha)` = top$gain_ha, `Loss (ha)` = top$loss_ha, `Net (ha)` = top$net_ha,
                  check.names = FALSE), 0)
```

Between 1985 and 2024, `r num(100 * im$change_fraction, 0)`% of the area changed
class. Almost all of that is quantity change (`r num(im$quantity_ha, 0)` ha),
meaning that one class grew by taking the place of another; only
`r num(im$allocation_ha, 0)` ha are swaps of position between classes. The forest
illustrates the picture well: only `r num(100 * f3$persistence_fraction, 0)`% of
the 1985 forest formation was still standing in 2024, and the
`r num(f3$gain_ha, 0)` ha that appeared elsewhere did not make up for the
`r num(f3$loss_ha, 0)` ha that were lost.

The net change of each class sums up, in a single plot, which classes gained and
which lost area over the period:

```{r net-change, fig.height=5.5}
change$change_plot
```

With `years = c(1985, 2004, 2024)`, the diagram gains a third column and each
pixel gets a trajectory: stable, changed once, changed twice or returned to its
original class:

```{r trajectories}
change3 <- land_change(maps, years = c(1985, 2004, 2024), language = "en")
```

```{r echo=FALSE}
tm <- change3$trajectory_metrics
labels <- c(stable = "Stable", changed_once = "Changed once",
            changed_twice = "Changed twice", returned = "Returned to the original class")
tabela(data.frame(Trajectory = labels[tm$type], `Area (ha)` = tm$area_ha,
                  `Share (%)` = 100 * tm$share, check.names = FALSE), 1)
```

## Adjacency between classes {-}

`land_to_graph()` looks at neighbourhoods: it counts the contacts between pixels
of different classes and builds the landscape network, in which each node is a
class and the thickness of each link is the number of contacts between them.
With `weight = "boundary"`, the thickness becomes the boundary length in metres.

```{r network, fig.height=6.5}
network <- land_to_graph(maps, year = 2024, language = "en")
network$plot
```

```{r include=FALSE}
nm <- network$node_metrics
hub <- nm[which.max(nm$degree), ]
```

In 2024, the most connected class is `r tolower(hub$class)`, which borders
`r hub$degree` classes along `r num(hub$boundary_m / 1000, 1)` km of edges.

## Boundaries and interfaces {-}

The adjacency matrix shows how many contacts there are between each pair of
classes; the diagonal (contacts of a class with itself) is left out unless
`include_self = TRUE`:

```{r heat-map, fig.height=6}
network$heatmap
```

Interfaces are the boundaries between pairs of classes, in kilometres. They are
where land use changes across the landscape and where edge effects concentrate:

```{r interfaces, fig.height=7}
network$edge_plot
```

```{r include=FALSE}
gm <- network$graph_metrics
em <- network$edge_metrics[order(-network$edge_metrics$boundary_m), ]
largest <- em[1, ]
forest <- em[em$from == 3 | em$to == 3, ]
```

The largest interface, between `r tolower(largest$from_class)` and
`r tolower(largest$to_class)`, adds up to `r num(largest$boundary_m / 1000, 1)` km
(`r num(100 * largest$share, 0)`% of the contacts between classes). The forest
borders `r nrow(forest)` classes, the main one being
`r tolower(ifelse(forest$from[1] == 3, forest$to_class[1], forest$from_class[1]))`.

`network$node_metrics` gives, for each class, degree (how many neighbouring
classes), strength (how many contacts), betweenness and neighbourhood entropy,
which is high when the class borders many others in similar proportions:

```{r echo=FALSE}
nm <- network$node_metrics[order(-network$node_metrics$strength), ]
tabela(data.frame(Class = nm$class, Degree = nm$degree, Strength = nm$strength,
                  Betweenness = nm$betweenness, `Neighbourhood entropy` = nm$neighbor_entropy,
                  check.names = FALSE), 2)
```

`network$graph_metrics` sums up the whole network: density (`r num(gm$density, 2)`),
transitivity (`r num(gm$transitivity, 2)`) and the share of contacts between
different classes (`r num(100 * gm$interclass_fraction, 0)`%), an indicator of how
patchy the landscape is.

The graph also has an interactive version, in which each class and each link show
their values on hover:

```{r interactive-network}
network$graph_plot
```
